header:
Is the AI boom wobbling?
OpenAI's $20B gap, explained

lines.text: A $20 billion gap shook the AI boom.
lines.say: A twenty billion dollar gap shook the A I boom.

lines.text: On Oct 8, 2026, the FT reported OpenAI told investors its yearly sales pace was about $50B.
lines.say: On October eighth, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI told investors its yearly sales pace was about fifty billion dollars.

lines.text: The number going around had been roughly $70B.
lines.say: The number going around had been roughly seventy billion.

lines.text: That same day, the Nasdaq fell 1.25%, its worst day since mid-August (CNN).
lines.say: That same day, the Nasdaq fell one and a quarter percent, its worst day since mid-August, CNN reported.

lines.text: Chipmakers took the biggest hit: the Philadelphia chip index fell 3.4%.
lines.say: Chipmakers took the biggest hit. The Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped three point four percent.

scene.headline: Chip stocks slide on OpenAI report

lines.text: And just two days earlier, on Oct 6, the Nasdaq had closed at a record, about 27,600.
lines.say: And only two days earlier, on October sixth, the Nasdaq had closed at a record, about twenty-seven thousand six hundred.

lines.text: So is the AI boom wobbling? Or did somebody just count differently?
lines.say: So is the A I boom wobbling? Or did somebody simply count differently?

lines.text: The gap reportedly comes down mostly to counting. But the selloff shows how much money rides on AI, including in your 401(k).
lines.say: The gap reportedly comes down mostly to counting. But the selloff shows how much money now rides on A I, including in your four oh one K.

lines.text: Coming up: the $20B gap, the $725B bet, lessons from 2000, and your 401(k).
lines.say: Coming up: the twenty billion dollar gap, the seven hundred twenty-five billion dollar bet, the lessons of two thousand, and your four oh one K.

lines.text: Chapter 1: The $20 billion gap.
lines.say: Let's start with that twenty billion dollar gap.

lines.text: OpenAI is private, so it doesn't publish audited results. It gives investors a run-rate.
lines.say: OpenAI is a private company, so it doesn't publish audited results. What it gives investors is a run-rate.

lines.text: A run-rate takes recent sales and multiplies them out to a full year.
lines.say: A run-rate takes recent sales and multiplies them out to a full year, as if every month looked like the latest one.

lines.text: Example: a lemonade stand sells $100 in its best month. Times 12, that's a $1,200 run-rate.
lines.say: Here's a made-up example. A lemonade stand sells a hundred dollars in its best month. Times twelve, that's a twelve hundred dollar run-rate.

lines.text: But if most months were slow, it might sell only $400 all year.
lines.say: But if most months were slow, the stand might sell only four hundred dollars all year.

lines.text: A run-rate is a snapshot of a good moment, not cash in the bank.
lines.say: So a run-rate is a snapshot of a good moment, not cash in the bank.

lines.text: OpenAI shows the same kind of gap. Its run-rate at the end of Sept was about $50B.
lines.say: OpenAI shows the same kind of gap. Its run-rate at the end of September was about fifty billion dollars.

lines.text: But its own forecast for all of 2026 revenue was $36B, the FT reported in Sept 2026.
lines.say: But its own forecast for all of twenty twenty-six revenue was thirty-six billion, the Financial Times reported in September.

lines.text: Now the $20B gap. A lot of AI is sold through cloud partners like Amazon and Google.
lines.say: Now, the twenty billion dollar gap. A lot of A I is sold through cloud partners, like Amazon and Google.

lines.text: Example: a customer pays $100 and the cloud partner keeps $20.
lines.say: In this made-up example, a customer pays a hundred dollars, and the cloud partner keeps twenty.

lines.text: Count it gross and you book $100. Count it net and you book $80. Per the FT and CNBC, Anthropic counts gross; OpenAI counts net.
lines.say: Count it gross, and you book the full hundred dollars. Count it net, and you book eighty. According to the F T and CNBC, rival Anthropic counts gross, and OpenAI counts net.

lines.text: A person familiar told CNBC the bigger figure included gross revenue from partners, to compare with Anthropic.
lines.say: A person familiar with the matter told CNBC the bigger figure included gross revenue from partners, so investors could compare it with Anthropic.

lines.text: CNN's source said the ~$70B figure didn't come from OpenAI at all.
lines.say: And CNN's source said the seventy billion dollar figure didn't come from OpenAI at all.

lines.text: And the growth is still there: OpenAI told investors its run-rate grew 77% in its third quarter.
lines.say: The growth is still there. OpenAI told investors its run-rate grew seventy-seven percent in its third quarter, the F T and CNBC reported.

lines.text: Reported run-rate: about $20B at the end of 2025, over $25B by Feb 2026...
lines.say: Look at the path, based on reports. About twenty billion dollars at the end of twenty twenty-five, and over twenty-five billion by February.

lines.text: ...over $40B in Aug 2026, and about $50B at the end of Sept.
lines.say: Then over forty billion in August, and about fifty billion at the end of September.

lines.text: That's more than double in nine months. Fast, just not as fast as the number going around.
lines.say: That's more than double in nine months. Fast growth, just not as fast as the number going around.

lines.text: So why did stocks drop? Some investors leaned on the bigger number, and many companies count on OpenAI's spending.
lines.say: So why did stocks drop over an accounting difference? Some investors had been leaning on the bigger number, and many companies count on OpenAI's spending.

lines.text: Oracle, which has a cloud deal with OpenAI, fell 5.5%. Intel fell 5.3%.
lines.say: Oracle, which has a big cloud deal with OpenAI, fell five and a half percent. Intel fell five point three percent.

lines.text: AMD fell 3.9% and Nvidia 2.9%. Higher oil and bond yields also weighed that day.
lines.say: A M D fell three point nine percent, and Nvidia two point nine. Higher oil prices and bond yields weighed on stocks that day too.

lines.text: Chapter 2: The $725 billion bet.
lines.say: Which brings us to the bigger story: the money being spent.

lines.text: Here's what the biggest tech spenders pour into big projects like data centers and chips.
lines.say: Here's what the biggest tech spenders pour into big projects like data centers and chips.

lines.text: About $154B in 2023, $241B in 2024 and $416B in 2025, incl. Oracle (Vanguard data).
lines.say: About one hundred fifty-four billion dollars in twenty twenty-three, two hundred forty-one billion in twenty twenty-four, and four hundred sixteen billion in twenty twenty-five, counting Oracle too, based on Vanguard's data.

lines.text: For 2026, just the big four (no Oracle) plan roughly $725B, per company guidance compiled by the FT.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-six, just the big four, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta, plan roughly seven hundred twenty-five billion dollars, based on company guidance compiled by the Financial Times. That's up about three quarters in one year.

lines.text: $725B a year is about $2B a day.
lines.say: That works out to about two billion dollars a day.

lines.text: Much of it goes to AI chips, servers and the buildings and power to run them.
lines.say: Much of it goes to A I chips, servers, and the buildings and power to run them.

lines.text: OpenAI spends heavily too: it expects to burn about $278B of cash from 2026 through 2030 (FT, Sept 2026).
lines.say: OpenAI is spending heavily too. In September, the F T reported it expects to burn through about two hundred seventy-eight billion dollars of cash from twenty twenty-six through twenty thirty.

lines.text: That's more than double the $122B it raised in March 2026, at an $852B valuation.
lines.say: That's more than double the one hundred twenty-two billion dollars it raised in March, at a valuation of eight hundred fifty-two billion.

lines.text: The FT reported it's on track to use up that cash by 2028, so revenue has to keep climbing fast.
lines.say: The F T reported it's on track to use up that cash by twenty twenty-eight. So its revenue has to keep climbing fast, or it needs more investors.

lines.text: Critics also point to what they call circular deals.
lines.say: Critics also point to what they call circular deals.

lines.text: That's when chipmakers invest in or lend to customers, who then buy their chips.
lines.say: That's when chipmakers invest in, or lend to, their own customers, who then turn around and buy their chips.

lines.text: Fortune and Axios have both covered that worry. UBS has argued the deals are manageable.
lines.say: Fortune and Axios have both covered that worry. Analysts at U B S, on the other hand, have argued the deals are manageable.

lines.text: The bet isn't only chips. It's electricity.
lines.say: And the bet isn't only chips. It's electricity.

lines.text: On Oct 6, 2026, Google signed a 20-year deal with Constellation for 890 MW of new nuclear capacity, from upgrades at existing plants.
lines.say: On October sixth, Google signed a twenty-year deal with Constellation Energy for eight hundred ninety megawatts of new nuclear capacity, from upgrades at plants that already exist.

lines.text: Constellation is investing more than $4.3B in the upgrades.
lines.say: Constellation is investing more than four point three billion dollars in those upgrades.

lines.text: That same week, the Energy Dept. offered Vistra a conditional loan of up to $4.2B.
lines.say: That same week, the Energy Department offered Vistra a conditional loan of up to four point two billion for its own nuclear upgrades.

lines.text: By one ING estimate, tech investment was about 36% of US economic growth in Q2 2026.
lines.say: It shows up in the whole economy too. By one estimate from the bank I N G, tech investment made up about thirty-six percent of US economic growth in the second quarter.

lines.text: That cuts both ways: more spending lifts growth; less would shrink that lift.
lines.say: That cuts both ways. When the spending grows, it lifts the economy. If it ever slowed, that lift would shrink too.

lines.text: It even shows up in trade: August 2026 imports hit a record, with $2.4B more in chips than July (BEA).
lines.say: It even shows up in trade. In August, US imports hit a record, including two point four billion dollars more in semiconductors than in July, the government reported.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Lessons from 2000.
lines.say: So have we seen something like this before? Sort of.

lines.text: On March 10, 2000, during the dot-com boom, the Nasdaq closed at a record 5,049.
lines.say: On March tenth, two thousand, at the height of the dot-com boom, the Nasdaq closed at a record of about five thousand forty-nine.

lines.text: By Oct 9, 2002, it had fallen about 78%.
lines.say: Then the bubble burst. By October ninth, two thousand two, it had fallen about seventy-eight percent.

lines.text: It didn't get back to that peak until April 2015.
lines.say: It didn't get back to that peak until April twenty fifteen, fifteen years later.

lines.text: Nasdaq: 5,049 at the top, 1,114 at the bottom.
lines.say: In numbers, that's about five thousand forty-nine at the top, and about one thousand one hundred fourteen at the bottom.

lines.text: Here's the twist: the internet was real. Many of the stock prices built on it weren't.
lines.say: Here's the twist. The internet was real. But many of the stock prices built on it ran far ahead of the profits.

lines.text: Take Cisco. It sold the networking gear the internet ran on, a bit like chipmakers today.
lines.say: Take Cisco. It sold the networking gear the internet ran on, a bit like the chipmakers of today.

lines.text: On March 27, 2000, it closed at a record $80.06 and was briefly the world's most valuable public company.
lines.say: On March twenty-seventh, two thousand, it closed at a record eighty dollars and six cents, and was briefly the most valuable public company in the world.

lines.text: The stock didn't close above that until Dec 10, 2025, at $80.25. About 25 years later.
lines.say: The stock didn't close above that until December tenth, twenty twenty-five, at eighty dollars and twenty-five cents. That's about twenty-five years later.

lines.text: Yet the business kept growing: revenue nearly quintupled after 1999.
lines.say: Yet the business kept growing. Its revenue nearly quintupled after nineteen ninety-nine.

lines.text: The price was the problem: 96.7x earnings in late 1999, about 19x expected earnings in Dec 2025.
lines.say: The price was the problem. In late nineteen ninety-nine, investors paid about ninety-seven times earnings. By December twenty twenty-five, it was about nineteen times expected earnings.

lines.text: The lesson isn't that AI is a bubble. Nobody knows that. A great business and a great stock price aren't the same thing.
lines.say: The lesson isn't that A I is a bubble. Nobody knows that. It's that a great business and a great stock price aren't the same thing.

lines.text: Then, Cisco sold the picks and shovels. Today, chipmakers like Nvidia play that role.
lines.say: Back then, Cisco sold the picks and shovels for the gold rush. Today, chipmakers like Nvidia play a similar role.

lines.text: One big difference: today's biggest spenders, like Microsoft and Alphabet, already make big profits.
lines.say: One big difference is that today's biggest spenders, like Microsoft and Alphabet, are already hugely profitable companies.

lines.text: But in a market this concentrated, a wobble in a few names moves everyone's fund.
lines.say: But there's a catch. In a market this concentrated, a wobble in a few names moves almost everyone's fund.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Your 401(k) and AI.
lines.say: So what does any of this have to do with your money?

lines.text: If you own an S&P 500 index fund, maybe inside a 401(k), you own a slice of this boom.
lines.say: If you own an S and P five hundred index fund, maybe inside a four oh one K, you already own a big slice of this boom.

lines.text: Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft now make up over 21% of the S&P 500, per Creative Planning (Oct 6, 2026).
lines.say: Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft now make up more than twenty-one percent of the index, according to Creative Planning.

lines.text: That's the most ever for three stocks. In the mid-1980s, IBM, AT&T and Exxon peaked at 13.4%.
lines.say: That's the most ever for three stocks. In the mid nineteen eighties, the top three, I B M, A T and T and Exxon, peaked at thirteen point four percent.

lines.text: Example: of every $100 in an S&P 500 fund, about $21 sits in those three companies.
lines.say: So in this example, out of every hundred dollars in the fund, about twenty-one dollars sits in just those three companies.

lines.text: If those three fell 10% together, the fund would drop about 2.1% from them alone, all else equal.
lines.say: If those three fell ten percent together, that alone would pull the fund down about two point one percent, all else equal.

lines.text: It works the same way going up.
lines.say: And it works exactly the same way on the way up.

lines.text: Nvidia alone is about 8.5% of the S&P 500 (early Oct 2026).
lines.say: Nvidia alone is about eight and a half percent of the index, based on fund holdings in early October.

lines.text: And many other names, from Oracle to power producers, are tied to AI spending too.
lines.say: And plenty of other names, from Oracle to the power producers, are tied to A I spending too.

lines.text: Constellation's stock jumped about 12% on Oct 6, the day of the Google deal.
lines.say: Constellation's stock, for example, jumped about twelve percent on October sixth, the day of the Google deal.

lines.text: When AI spending grows, chipmakers, power producers and builders benefit. If it got cut, they'd feel it first.
lines.say: When A I spending grows, chipmakers, power producers and builders benefit. If it ever got cut, those same suppliers, and index funds heavy in them, would feel it.

lines.text: Some funds weight every company equally, about 0.2% each in an equal-weight S&P 500 fund.
lines.say: There are also equal-weight versions of the S and P five hundred, which hold each company at about zero point two percent.

lines.text: That's not advice, just how the two designs differ.
lines.say: That's not advice, just how the two designs differ.

lines.text: None of this predicts where stocks go next. It shows how much of a typical retirement account rides on one theme.
lines.say: None of this predicts where stocks go next. It just shows how much of a typical retirement account now rides on one theme.

lines.text: Chapter 5: What to watch.
lines.say: So what's on the calendar?

lines.text: Oct 14: September inflation report (BLS).
lines.say: On October fourteenth, the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases September's inflation report.

lines.text: Higher rates make far-off profits worth less to investors today.
lines.say: That matters because higher inflation and interest rates make far-off profits worth less to investors today.

lines.text: Oct 28: the Fed's next rate decision, after its Sept 2026 hike.
lines.say: On October twenty-eighth, the Fed announces its next rate decision, after raising rates in September.

lines.text: Late Oct: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon usually report. Watch their spending plans.
lines.say: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon usually report in late October. A key number is whether they raise or trim their spending plans.

lines.text: And Nvidia usually reports in late November, a read on whether chip orders keep coming.
lines.say: And Nvidia usually reports in late November, which shows whether the chip orders are still coming in.

lines.text: The one number to watch: that ~$725B of planned spending.
lines.say: If you remember one number, make it that seven hundred twenty-five billion dollars of planned spending. It shows whether the boom is speeding up or slowing down.

lines.text: And watch whether OpenAI shares more official numbers. Until then, run-rates are what it tells investors.
lines.say: And watch whether OpenAI shares more official numbers. Until a company publishes audited results, run-rates are simply what it tells investors.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap.
lines.say: Let's recap.

lines.text: OpenAI's run-rate was about $50B, not the ~$70B widely reported.
lines.say: OpenAI's run-rate was about fifty billion dollars, not the roughly seventy billion that was widely reported.

lines.text: The gap is reportedly mostly gross vs net counting, and growth was still 77% in Q3.
lines.say: The gap is reportedly mostly gross versus net counting, and its run-rate still grew seventy-seven percent in the third quarter.

lines.text: Big Tech plans to spend roughly $725B in 2026, much of it on AI.
lines.say: Big Tech plans to spend roughly seven hundred twenty-five billion dollars in twenty twenty-six, much of it on A I.

lines.text: And three stocks are over 21% of the S&P 500, so many 401(k)s ride on it.
lines.say: And three stocks make up more than twenty-one percent of the S and P five hundred, so many four oh one Ks ride on it.

lines.text: Real growth, giant bills, and a market more concentrated than ever: the AI boom in October 2026.
lines.say: Real growth, giant bills, and a market more concentrated than ever. That's the A I boom in October twenty twenty-six.

lines.say: If this helped, subscribe for the week's biggest money story, explained on a whiteboard.

post.yt_desc:
A $20 billion gap shook the AI boom: on Oct 8, 2026, the Financial Times reported OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue was about $50 billion, not the roughly $70 billion widely reported, and the Nasdaq had its worst day since mid-August. This video explains run-rates and gross vs net counting, follows the roughly $725 billion Big Tech plans to spend in 2026 (including new nuclear power deals), and compares today with the 2000 dot-com bust and Cisco's 25-year wait. It also shows why three stocks making up over 21% of the S&P 500 puts the AI boom inside many 401(k)s, and lists the dates to watch next.

Sources: Financial Times, CNBC, CNN and TechCrunch (Oct 8, 2026); Financial Times via Reuters (Sept 19, 2026); Bloomberg (Aug 2026); The Information via Reuters (Mar 2026); AP market data (Oct 6, 2026); Vanguard hyperscaler capex data; Financial Times capex tally and Forbes (Oct 7, 2026); Fortune; Axios; UBS; Google and Constellation (Oct 6, 2026); US Department of Energy (Oct 2026); BEA/Census (Oct 6, 2026); ING (2026); Barchart and Sherwood News (Dec 2025); Creative Planning via Yahoo Finance and Benzinga (Oct 6, 2026); BLS and Federal Reserve calendars.

News and education, not financial advice.
